content: Aedes aegypti, commonly referred to as the yellow fever mosquito, is a species of mosquito capable of transmitting viruses such as dengue fever, chikungunya, and yellow fever, among others. A group of researchers has proposed renaming this species to Stegomyia aegypti, but this suggestion has not yet gained widespread acceptance within the scientific community. This mosquito can be identified by its distinctive white markings, although other mosquito species may exhibit similar but slightly different patterns. It is predominantly found in tropical regions, with some presence in the southeastern United States, particularly in the lower half of Florida. However, its population in these areas appears to have been reduced due to competition with the introduced species Aedes albopictus. In terms of physical appearance, Aedes aegypti is relatively small, measuring approximately 3 to 4 millimeters in length. Its body is predominantly black, with white spots on the head and body, as well as white rings on its legs. The genome of Aedes aegypti was fully sequenced and published on May 17, 2007. This genomic mapping effort aimed to facilitate research into insecticides and explore potential genetic modifications to prevent the spread of diseases. This species was the second mosquito to have its genome fully sequenced, following Anopheles gambiae. The genome consists of 38 billion base pairs and approximately 15,419 protein-coding genes. The genetic data suggest that Aedes aegypti diverged from Drosophila melanogaster (the common fruit fly) around 250 million years ago and from Anopheles gambiae approximately 150 million years ago. To prevent the spread of diseases such as dengue fever, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends the use of mosquito repellents containing DEET (N,N-diethyl-meta-toluamide). The CDC also notes that while Aedes aegypti may feed at any time, it primarily bites humans during the hours between a few hours after dawn and shortly after sunset. The mosquito prefers to breed in stagnant water, such as that found in flower vases, uncovered barrels, buckets, and discarded tires. However, the most hazardous breeding sites are wet shower floors and toilet bowls, as these allow the mosquitoes to reproduce within residential areas. A 1978 photograph from the Public Health Image Library (PHIL) illustrates the cracked surface of dredged spoil deposits, which, when wet, served as oviposition and breeding sites for a population of Aedes sollicitans mosquitoes.
